LESSON_ONE_GRAMMAR_FIVE.titleTraditional: 主語 + 動詞 + 受詞
LESSON_ONE_GRAMMAR_FIVE.learnerPromise: Build a complete sentence with a subject, a verb, and an object, in that order.
LESSON_ONE_GRAMMAR_FIVE.explanation: A Chinese sentence follows one order: Subject → Verb → Object. Put the subject first, then the verb, then the object. The object is the person or thing the verb affects.

teachingGlossary.meaning: not; goes right before the verb
to like; the verb in this sentence pattern
“to be”; links someone to an identity. Do not put it before a verb

discoveryLab.title: Let the sentence grow one meaning block at a time
discoveryLab.description: Chinese listeners build the message in the same order that they hear it. Each step answers one more question.

choices.label: 1 · Subject
choices.note: The subject comes first. The listener knows who the sentence is about, but still waits for the verb.

choices.label: 2 · Verb
choices.note: The verb comes second. The listener still needs the object — the person or thing that is liked.

choices.label: 3 · Object
choices.note: 臺灣 is the object. Subject → Verb → Object completes the sentence.

choices.label: Repair · no 是
choices.traditional: 我是喜歡臺灣。 → 我喜歡臺灣。
choices.simplified: 我是喜欢台湾。 → 我喜欢台湾。
choices.pinyin: Wǒ shì xǐhuān Táiwān. → Wǒ xǐhuān Táiwān.
choices.note: 喜歡 is already the verb. Do not add 是 before it.

discoveryLab.takeaway: Build the sentence in order: Subject → Verb → Object. Put 不 right before the verb to make it negative.

sentenceSpine.title: Now switch the meaning without rebuilding the sentence
sentenceSpine.description: Keep the three slots in place and attach 不 directly to the verb.
notes: 不 stays right before the verb: 不喜歡.
Verbs like 喜歡 and 愛 do not need 是.

items.question: In English I say “I am liking Taiwan.” Do I need 是?
items.answer: No. 喜歡 already carries the feeling — it never takes 是. Keep 是 for names and identities, like 我是日本人.

items.question: Where does 不 go to say I do not like something?
items.answer: Right before the verb: 不喜歡. Never after the verb or before the object.

right.english: I do not like Miss Wang.

items.question: Can the person or thing come first, like “Dad and Mom I love”?
items.answer: No. Chinese keeps the order Subject → Verb → Object. The object goes last.

examples.teachingNote: The second part does not repeat 我.

text.traditional: 我喜歡李小姐，不喜歡王小姐。
text.simplified: 我喜欢李小姐，不喜欢王小姐。
text.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuān Lǐ xiǎojiě, bù xǐhuān Wáng xiǎojiě.
text.english: I like Miss Li, but I do not like Miss Wang.

examples.teachingNote: 什麼 stands in for the thing you like.

text.traditional: 你喜歡什麼？
text.pinyin: Nǐ xǐhuān shénme?
text.english: What do you like?

examples.teachingNote: One verb can take two objects.

text.traditional: 我愛爸爸、媽媽。
text.pinyin: Wǒ ài bàba, māma.
text.english: I love Dad and Mom.
